Tromino Puzzle

InductionCountingArea

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)

Game: One square of the board is missing. Cover every other square with L-shaped pieces of three squares.
How to play: Click three free squares in an L, each next to the one before, to place a piece. Use Remove last when you trap yourself.

Look for the math

A square board of size 2n × 2n has one square taken away. However big the board and wherever the gap, the rest can be covered exactly by L-trominoes — three unit squares in an L. That is Solomon Golomb's theorem, and this page is the manual version: the applet gives no hints, so the proof is also the best way to play.

Cut the board into four

Draw the two middle lines. The gap lies in exactly one of the four equal quarters. Place one L around the centre covering one square in each of the other three quarters. Now all four quarters have a gap: the real one in its quarter, and the square taken by the centre L in the other three. Each quarter is a smaller copy of the same problem.

Repeat. The boards halve each time — 32, 16, 8, 4, 2 — and a 2 × 2 board with one square gone is exactly one L. So the process always ends, and it never needs a search. This is mathematical induction.

How many pieces?

A 2n × 2n board has 4n squares. One is missing, so 4n − 1 squares remain, and each L covers 3. The finished board therefore has (4n − 1) / 3 pieces. The page shows 2 × 2, 4 × 4, 8 × 8, 16 × 16 and 32 × 32 boards: that is 1, 5, 21, 85 and 341 pieces. The logic test plays Golomb's construction on every gap of every board up to 16 × 16 — 340 boards — and checks that the count always comes out right and that every square but the gap is covered once.

Is the answer unique?

On the 2 × 2 and 4 × 4 boards it is. The test counts every possible tiling and finds exactly one for each of the 16 gaps on a 4 × 4 board, always the one Golomb's construction builds. From 8 × 8 on there are many: the test finds more than one covering of an 8 × 8 board with the same gap. So the small boards are a proof you can copy, and the large ones are a real choice.

Why careless play strands squares

An L always covers three squares, so the total left to cover is always a multiple of three. A pocket of one or two squares can therefore never be filled on its own: the remaining count is wrong, and no L fits. That is what the page means by "1 and 2 squares pockets". The way out is Remove last: take pieces back until the pocket merges with free space, then follow the quarter-by-quarter plan.

On a 8 × 8 board, try Golomb's plan: put the first L around the centre, then treat each 4 × 4 quarter as its own small puzzle. Switch to Blocks to see the four orientations in four colours.
